FALSIFIABLE
Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample.
Let $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a set of $n$ points with no three on a line. Does $A$ determine at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances? In fact, must there exist a single point from which there are at least $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ distinct distances?
#1082: [Er75f,p.101][Er87b][Er97e]
geometry | 
distances
A conjecture of Szemerédi, who proved this with $n/2$ replaced by $n/3$. More generally, Szemerédi gave a simple proof that if there are no $k$ points on a line then some point determines $\gg n/k$ distinct distances (a weak inverse result to the distinct distance problem [89]).
This is a stronger form of [93]. The second question is a stronger form of [982].
Szemerédi's proof is unpublished, but given in [Er75f].
In [Er75f] Erdős asks whether, given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with no three on a line, do they determine $\gg n$ distances? Altman proved the answer is yes if the points form the vertices of a convex polyhedron (see [660] for a stronger form of this), and Szemerédi proved the answer is yes if there are no four points on a plane.
The second stronger question has a negative answer: there is a construction of $8$ points such that each point has exactly three distinct distances to the others. This first appeared in the literature in a paper of Erdős and Fishburn [ErFi97b], where they credit the construction to Harborth. This configuration is studied in detail by Fishburn [Fi02].
(This construction was later found by DeepMind. An earlier construction was also given by Xichuan in the comments, who gave a set of $42$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$, with no three on a line, such that each point determines only $20$ distinct distances.)
Additional thanks to: Stijn Cambie, Sharvil Kesarwani, and Xichuan

 The first question holds for all $n \le 15$.
The thread so far concerns the second question (must some single point see $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ distinct distances?), which Harborth's $H_8$ refutes; BorisAlexeev notes in this thread that the main conjecture is still open. Worth saying that $H_8$ satisfies the first question, determining $4 = \lfloor 8/2 \rfloor$ distances in total even though no point sees more than $3$.
Write $g(k)$ for the largest number of points in the plane determining at most $k$ distinct distances (the same as the standard exactly-$k$ maximum, since the known values increase), and $h(k)$ for the same with no three collinear. A counterexample on $n$ points with $k$ distances needs $n \ge 2k+2$, so the first question is exactly $h(k) \le 2k+1$ for every $k$. The regular $(2k+1)$-gon gives the reverse, so the question is $h(k) = 2k+1$ with no slack at any $k$, which seems to me the main obstruction.
Since $h(k) \le g(k)$, the published $g(1),\dots,g(6) = 3,5,7,9,12,13$ settle every $k \le 6$ except $k = 5$, where $g(5) = 12$. Shinohara's uniqueness for the maximum $5$-distance set closes that case: the extremal set is the Eisenstein configuration, which contains $18$ collinear triples, and nothing smaller can reach $12$ points since $g(4) = 9$, so $h(5) = 11$. Hence $h(k) = 2k+1$ for all $k \le 6$, and $n \le 15$ follows in three lines.
On Altman, who is cited on this page for the three-dimensional case (convex polyhedra): his planar theorem bears directly on the first question and does not seem to have been noted here. Altman ("On a problem of P. Erdős", Amer. Math. Monthly 70 (1963), 148-157) proved that every convex $n$-gon determines at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ distinct distances. Convex position forces no three collinear, so that is exactly the first question restricted to convex position, settled since 1963. Any counterexample must therefore be non-convex.
For comparison, the published lower bound for this question, Szemerédi's $\lceil (n-1)/3 
ceil$ as recorded in Sheffer's survey, reaches $\lfloor n/2 
floor$ only at $n = 5$. The smallest conceivable counterexample is $n = 16$ with $7$ distances, open only because $g(7)$ is unknown.

 Here is a picture of the configuration of eight points. In words, one description of the configuration might be: Let four of the points be vertices of a square. Then, on each side of the square, construct an equilateral triangle. The remaining four points are the other vertices of those triangles. (The triangles can either all face outward or all face inward, but the resulting configuration is the same in both cases.)
Also, note that the main conjecture is still open. Both this construction, and the one by eigensolver, disprove the second/"stronger" part of the conjecture.

 Following @StijnC's idea, I seem to have found a counterexample to the second question. It consists of $42$ points: 
Image Link
GeoGebra Link
This counterexample is composed of two concentric regular $N$-gons ($N = 21$), denoted as $A_1A_2\dots A_N$ and $B_1B_2\dots B_N$ counterclockwisely, with inner and outer radius ratio equal to $r_0=\frac12\left(1-\sqrt{5-8\cos\frac{2\pi}{7}}\right)=0.4450418679\dots$, a root of $x^3-x^2-2x+1=0$. This set of points satisfies $|A_1A_4|=|A_1B_4|$ and $|B_1B_{10}|=|B_1 A_5|$, which degenerates distances, and for any $B_k$, the line $A_1 B_k$ does not pass through any other points. Due to symmetry, each point determines only $N−1 = 20$ distinct distances, thus constituting a counterexample to the second problem.
The method I used involved solving quadratic equations in terms of $r$, of the form $|A_1 B_i| = |A_1 A_j|$ and $|B_1 B_k| = |B_1 A_l|$, obtaining solution sets $R_1$ and $R_2$, and then selecting $r$ from their intersection such that no three points are collinear. However, due to precision errors, I might have misjudged the solutions. I would be immensely grateful if someone could help verify this.
By the way, all $(N, r)$ pairs I found are of the form:
$$(42k+21, r_0),\quad (42k+21, 1-r_0)\quad (k\in\mathbb{N})$$
